title: TB1-10491
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (hereafter known as the principal claimant), XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX, all citizens of Croatia, claim refugee protection pursuant to Sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA). XXXX XXXX was appointed the Designated Representative for the minor children.
The specifics of the claim are set out in the narrative to the claimants Personal Information Forms2 (PIF) and amendments; however the following is a summary.

The claimants allege that they have faced periodic discrimination and persecution in Croatia due to their ethnicity. The principal claimant (PC) specifically fears certain individuals, and believes that they are targeting him due to his Croatian Bosnian background, and involvement in the Serbian military. The claimants resided in the small town of XXXX, outside of XXXX for their entire time in Croatia.

The discrimination that the claimants faced included racial slurs, bullying of their son's in school, and discrimination in the workplace. Both adult claimants have a long work history in Croatia and worked up until their departure to Canada, though XXXX alleges discrimination in trying to secure a job as a XXXX. Their children remained in school until coming to Canada.

The PC crossed into Bosnia on average twice a year to visit family in Bosnia, and did so one month prior to coming to Canada. The PC fears two specific individuals from his town whom he states have not forgotten the war. His problems with them began in 2005, when he approached them as their children had been teasing his son for being Serbian. Following his discussion with these parents the claimants had graffiti written on their building, and their children were being intimidated by one of the parents. The PC reported this to the police.
In 2011 his son was assaulted by unknown hooligans and robbed. This was also reported to the police and while the police tried to find photographs matching the description, they could not.
The claimants decided to leave Croatia following the XXXX 2011 event, and in XXXX 2011, came to Canada and filed for refugee protection.
I find that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
The determinative issue in this claim is state protection in Croatia; however significant subjective fear issues arise with the claimants' evidence and they failed to establish past persecution.
Counsel's post hearing submissions were received and considered.3 Identity
The claimants' identities as citizens of Croatia are established by their testimony and by the personal identity documents filed, including their Croatian passports.4 Establishment of the Claim

To be found a Convention refugee, a claimant must have a well-founded fear of future persecution. A distinction can and should be made between persecution, on the one hand, and discrimination or harassment on the other; with persecution being characterized by the greater seriousness of the mistreatment it involves.5 A finding of discrimination is within the jurisdiction of the Refugee Protection Division.6
The panel notes that cumulative acts of discrimination might indeed constitute persecution,7 in certain circumstances.

The UNHCR Handbook on Procedures and Criteria for Determining Refugee Status notes that: Differences in the treatment of various groups do indeed exist to a greater or lesser extent in many societies. People who receive less favourable treatment as a result of such differences are not necessarily victims of persecution. It is only in certain circumstances that discrimination will amount to persecution. This would be so if measures of discrimination lead to consequences of a seriously prejudicial nature for the person concerned, e.g. serious restrictions on his right to earn his livelihood, his right to practice his religion, or his access to normally available educational facilities.8

Objective evidence indicates that the situation of ethnic minorities in Croatia has improved in the past 10 years, though minorities still face some harassment and discrimination. Human rights groups and religious leaders report that overall ethnic and religious relations remain stable, with some noted sporadic violence and threats directed against all religious groups.9

Ethnic Serbs are the largest minority in Croatia, constituting around 4.5 per cent of the population. It is estimated that the numbers are far greater as many Serbs spend long periods of time outside of Croatia and are not present for census taking.10

There is some evidence that some Serbs have faced discrimination in housing, however these claimants had housing in XXXX, Croatia consistently from the date of their arrival.11 No evidence was provided at the hearing on a restriction of access to housing.

Similarly, there is no persuasive evidence of any restriction or denial of an education, opportunity to earn a livelihood or evidence of any restriction on the practice of religion in the short time that these claimants resided in Croatia.

The two minor children were in school until relocating to Canada, and while the claimants allege that they experienced periodic bullying, there is no persuasive evidence of any restriction to access an educational facility.12

XXXX alleges that she experienced discrimination in finding employment as a XXXX in Croatia. She indicates that she applied to the only XXXX in her area, and that she was turned down as she is Serbian. She did not file any formal complaints about discrimination, and was able to secure other employment consistently in XXXX until departure to Canada, from 2001-2011.

While it may be disappointing when one cannot practice a profession where credentials come from another country, not finding employment in ones chosen field is not persuasive evidence of a substantial restriction on the right to earn a livelihood. It is not uncommon for professionals to have to redirect their careers to adjust to changing economic situations, or to a new country location. While the documents do confirm that in some areas Serbs are subject to difficulties in accessing employment, the PC's evidence was not persuasive that her problems in securing employment were due to ethnicity.13

The claimants allege harassment by known offenders in the town of XXXX. I find their choice to remain located in the same small town, their long delay in departure from the start of events, and their frequent reavailments of Croatia severely undermine their subjective fear and the establishment of persecution at all.

Persecution is defined in refugee law to be the inflicting of harm with repetition or persistence.14 The PC fears a specific individual that he chose not to report to the police, and provided evidence of racial slurs and intimidation of his sons and wife dating back to 2005. Subjective fear issues are raised by his evidence and conduct and I do not find that the claimants established harassment or discrimination amounting to persecution. Subjective Fear

By definition, a Convention refugee is someone who has a well-founded fear of persecution. Fear is, by its very nature, subjective, while the well-foundedness of that fear is an objective matter. Both subjective and objective components are required to meet the definition15, and even a lack of evidence going to the subjective element of the claim is in itself sufficient for the claim to fail.16

The PC's evidence presents a situation of multiple reavailments, and a failure to relocate away from a small town of alleged persecution over an extended period of time. The evidence of the claimants is more reflective of a situation of country shopping, rather than of genuine refugees in need of international protection.

Return to the country of nationality may indicate that a well-founded fear of persecution is lacking where the claimant's conduct is inconsistent with such fear.17 The PC indicates multiple trips to Bosnia to visit friends and returns to Croatia; his last reavailment was just prior to coming to Canada. Similar evidence was provided by his wife, the joined claimant.

The conduct of frequent returns to the country of alleged persecution is conduct inconsistent with a genuine subjective fear under the law. The PC was asked to explain his reavailments in light of evidence of persecution in XXXX, and he stated that he had to go and visit his mother. I do not find it reasonable that one who genuinely fears persecution would be traveling and returning to the same area of persecution over an extended time. An adverse finding is drawn on the level of alleged subjective fear.

Subjective fear issues also arise with the evidence on their failure to relocate in Croatia. The PC was asked why he and his family did not leave the small village and relocate to a bigger, more cosmopolitan city, and the PC indicated that in each town, there are groups of people bothering each other. He stated that it is the same in Serbia and Bosnia also. I do not find it reasonable that the PC and his family would remain in their small town, if in such danger. They had access to larger, cosmopolitan cities where they could be away from their bothersome neighbours and be more anonymous. The claimants had the sophistication and resources to relocate to Canada, it would have been reasonable for them to try a more local solution prior to seeking international `protection. An adverse finding is drawn on their subjective fear. Finding

The claimants failed to establish that they will face any persecution on return to Croatia, or that they suffered past persecution in Croatia. While the PC alleges to fear specific individuals in his small town, he also indicates that the problems were periodic.

The claimants did not establish with either their conduct or evidence, the level of subjective fear associated with a genuine refugee in need of international protection and as a result the claim under s. 96 of the IRPA fails.

While I do not find that the claimants established more than a mere possibility of persecution on return to Croatia, even had the claimants established a claim under s. 96 or 97(1) of the IRPA, they failed to rebut the presumption of state protection in Croatia today. State Protection

There is a presumption that countries are capable of protecting its citizens, and this underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available. The Board is not obliged to prove that Croatia can offer the claimant effective state protection, rather, the claimant bears the legal burden of rebutting the presumption that adequate state protection exists by adducing clear and convincing evidence which satisfies the Board on a balance of probabilities.18

In other words, to rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide "clear and convincing" evidence of the state's inability to protect its citizens.19 The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.20

In this regard, the onus is high on a claimant coming from a democratic country. A claimant must show that they have taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek protection, taking into account the context of the country of origin, the steps taken and the claimant's interactions with the authorities.21

A state, unless in complete breakdown, is presumed to be capable of protecting its citizens, and international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant cannot obtain protection domestically. A claimant is required to approach the state for protection if protection might reasonably be forthcoming or, alternatively, if it is objectively reasonable for the claimant to have sought protection.22

The PC indicates that in 2005 he reported to the police that his sons had been bullied. He took matters into his own hand and also approached the parents of one of the children, which led to problems for his family. The claimant identifies that there is just one police station in XXXX, and this is where he reported.

The PC states that when his son was assaulted in 2011 in XXXX, while going to high school, he attended with his son at the police. He could not identify his attackers and the police indicated that if the PC was concerned about another event, he should escort his son to school. The PC was not satisfied. The PC has not provided any police reports in support of these events. Neither the PC, or his wife have reported any problems anywhere else, or followed up with the police where not satisfied with their action.

The PC indicates that he fears a specific individual, XXXX XXXX, who has assaulted him in the past; however he failed to report this to the police. When asked why he would fail to report a known assailant, the PC indicated that some of the police are corrupt and he feared reporting and having further problems. In refugee law the adequacy of state protection cannot rest on the subjective fear of the claimant23; and a claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state.24 Furthermore, there cannot be said to be a failure of state protection where a government has not been given an opportunity to respond.25

I have considered whether or not these claimants took all reasonable steps in their circumstances to seek protection and, in view of these principles, I find that the claimants have not provided the requisite clear and convincing evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, state protection in Croatia is inadequate; or that they exhausted all avenues before fleeing to Canada.

The objective evidence confirms that Croatia is functioning, and that there has been no breakdown of state institutions. Croatia is an electoral democracy. Both the 2009-2010 presidential poll and the 2007 parliamentary elections were deemed free and fair. The 153-member unicameral parliament (Sabor) is composed of 140 members from geographical districts, 8 of which represent ethnic minorities, and a variable number representing Croatians living abroad. All members are elected to four-year terms. The president of the republic, who serves as head of state, is elected by popular vote for a maximum of two five-year terms. The prime minister is appointed by the president but must be approved by the parliament. The national police have primary responsibility for national security; in times of disorder, the prime minister and the president may call upon the military to provide security. The intelligence service is under the authority of the prime minister and the president. An independent oversight board monitors intelligence service performance.26

The constitution guarantees freedoms of expression and the press. While these rights are generally respected in practice, reporters remain vulnerable to political pressure, and journalists have alleged that the media are becoming increasingly beholden to the interests of powerful advertisers.27

Freedom of religion is guaranteed by the constitution.28 The constitution provides for freedoms of association and assembly. A variety of both international and domestic non-governmental organizations (NGOs) operate in Croatia without governmental interference or harassment. The constitution allows workers to form and join trade unions, and they do so freely. Approximately 64 percent of the workforce is unionized. Despite these freedoms, the International Trade Union Confederation criticized Croatia's 2009 Act on the Basis for Wages in Public Services for endangering the right to collective bargaining. The position of trade unions in the country has also been weakened by the recent global economic crisis, which has forced some trade union organizations to temporarily suspend their participation in the state's Economic and Social Council, an advisory body to the Croatian government which coordinates dialogue and harmonizes policies between employers, trade unions, and the government.

Respect for minority rights in Croatia has improved over the past decade, but various forms of harassment and discrimination persist. Ethnic minorities, particularly Serbs, remain under represented at several levels of government and in the civil administration.

Returning Serbs are still harassed by the local population, although the frequency of such incidents is on the decline. Croatian authorities have taken steps to protect religious and ethnic minorities. Constitutional protections against discrimination apply to all minorities.29

Minority groups are guaranteed seats in the Croatian parliament and in some areas are guaranteed proportional representation in public service employment.30 The National Minority Council receives significant government funding for minority cultural programs31, and legislation entitles national minorities to primary and secondary education in their own language.32

The government also funds employers to hire minority workers.33 The 2009 Anti-Discrimination Act makes the ombudsman the central body for promoting equality.34 The Croatian ombudsman became the central body for promoting equality, with the passage of anti discrimination legislation in January, 2009. The claimants have never approached the Ombudsman for assistance. The PC indicated in questioning that he was aware of the Ombudsman in Bosnia but not Croatia.

It is noted in the United Nations, Human Rights Council Report that: "The principle of equality was enshrined in the Constitution and enjoyed special legal protection, and the Criminal Code recognized the concept of hate crimes. The 2008 Antidiscrimination Act and the National Plan for Combating Discrimination (2008-2013) were other instruments to counter discrimination. In 2010, Croatia had established a new Working Group to monitor hate crimes at the national level. Special efforts were devoted to combating discrimination against minorities, including the Serb and the Roma minorities and lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons. Special attention was being paid both to awareness-raising activities and the strengthening of institutional capacity. Politicians were increasingly spreading the message of tolerance and reconciliation. Recent trends had indicated an increase in the investigation of hate crimes. Criminal acts directed against journalists, particularly attacks on their physical integrity, were treated with the utmost seriousness and tended to be characterized as grave crimes under the Criminal Code. A number of assaults against journalists had resulted in criminal charges, as recently demonstrated through the first-instance judgement in respect of the killings of media professionals Pukanic and Franjic."35

For there to be adequate state protection, there needs to be signs of effectiveness of programs as well. The government's actions have had concrete results. A 2008 European Union progress report notes that police investigations of ethnically-motivated incidents have improved, although too few cases end in prosecutions.36 Adequate political representation of minorities has been achieved in some local and regional assemblies.37 In other cases, individuals who committed ethnically-motivated crimes were arrested, charged, and convicted38 and the situation of minorities in general has improved.39

None of this means that Croatia provides perfect protection to its citizens, including ethnic and religious minorities. Members of minorities are still confronted with harassment and discrimination.40 Some sources allege slow or ineffective reaction by the authorities to allegations of discrimination or violence against minorities, and investigative and prosecutorial actions have been criticized as slow.41 The government does not always observe the law requiring proportional minority representation in public service employment.42

Lastly, it is noted by the United Nations Human Rights Council report that Croatia has developed an advanced human rights protection system which is based on meeting international human rights standards.43 This is critical as Croatia has joined the European Union.

The objective evidence regarding state protection for individuals such as the claimants is mixed, and as such, is not a clear and convincing rebuttal of the presumption of state protection, as required.44

It is not for the panel to set out clear and convincing evidence to support the presumption of state protection, it is for the claimants to provide such evidence to rebut the presumption. Neither the mixed objective evidence nor the claimants' own evidence is a clear and convincing rebuttal of state protection.
The panel finds that adequate state protection is available to the claimants in their country, and as such, they are not entitled to or in need of Canada's surrogate protection.
The claimants have not established a well founded fear of persecution, with their evidence or conduct, and have failed to rebut the presumption of state protection.

Therefore the claims of XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX are denied.
